AgriDash node, firmware for the Raspberry Pi Pico, C++17

This page is running the firmware.

Not a video and not a mock-up. The C++ that ships to the board is compiled, unmodified, to a small WebAssembly engine and is sampling a sensor right now, on a wire you can break. The chart below is being drawn from what it reports. Pull the sensor, short the data line, hang the main loop, and watch what a node does when it is built to fail safely.

    Every point on this chart is a value the firmware reported. Where it reported none, the chart is left blank and marked.

      The binary that ships

      Everything above runs the firmware's logic as WebAssembly. This goes one step further: it takes agri_node.uf2, the exact file that is copied onto a Raspberry Pi Pico, and boots it on an emulated RP2040 processor, instruction by instruction. The Pico SDK starts up, enumerates over USB, and talks I²C to a second copy of the simulated sensor on the same bench.

      Not running.

      The board is not powered. Press the button above to boot agri_node.uf2.

      When it is running, each of its measurements is compared with the WebAssembly engine's for the same moment.

      Shown here: start-up, sampling, the air you set, an unplugged sensor, a power cycle. Not shown here: the stuck bus and the watchdog reset. The emulator has no pin-level model of the wire and does not reset the chip, so those two are demonstrated above on the WebAssembly engine and are checked on a real board. The emulator is rp2040js by Uri Shaked (MIT).

      The field

      One node is a demonstration. Here are 1,024 of them: each cell is its own instance of the release's sampler, with its own sensor, wire, watchdog and serial link. Weather and faults roll across the field. An oracle that knows the truth of the simulation checks every line every node writes against the specification. Paint faults onto the field and try to make one node report a number it did not measure.

      On the glass: a filled square is a healthy node, coloured by its temperature; a cross is a fault; a ring is an absent sensor; an exclamation mark is an out-of-range reading; z is a hung node; a dot is a node with no host; a blue wash is the storm.

      What the oracle checks on every record
      1. The line is valid JSON, is at most 256 bytes, and carries protocol version 1.
      2. A value is present if and only if the status is ok.
      3. A status of ok means the sensor really completed a measurement, the air really was inside the sensor's range, and the reported numbers match the simulated air to within the encoder's rounding (0.006 °C, 0.3 Pa, 0.06 %).
      4. up_ms is exactly the time since that node's last boot.
      5. seq rises by exactly one per period; after a dropped link the gap equals the number of lines that had no host.
      6. A boot record names the true reset cause (watchdog after a hang, power_on after a brown-out) and the true state of the sensor.
      7. A node whose bus has shown no trouble for one re-probe interval (30 s) does not report a fault.

      The node's memory

      This is the bench node's actual memory at the instant it handed its last line to the serial port: the bytes around the encoder's fixed 256-byte buffer, on the stack. There is no heap. The highlighted bytes are the line you can read in the console above.

          What is real on this page
          
  
          
    
          RealThe node's logic: the sampler, the BME280 driver with the datasheet's compensation formulas, and the bounded JSON encoder. These are the release's core/ sources, compiled without modification. 
          
    
          SimulatedThe sensor chip (a register-level model with the datasheet example's calibration, which converts the air you set into raw readings), the two wires, the millisecond clock, the watchdog timer and the serial port. On the board these are the Pico SDK's drivers; here they are about a hundred lines of JavaScript that you can read in this page's source.
